Outcome: Depression cases (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: no effect
Claim: 25OHD levels did not differ significantly between patients treated for depression and healthy controls.
Sentence: "The level of 25OHD and 1,25(OH)2D3 did not differ significantly between the examined groups."
Measured as: depression (patients treated for depression vs healthy controls)
Population: 99 patients aged 46.9 ± 11 years treated for depression and 45 healthy subjects
Intervention: Not applicable (observational; serum 25OHD measured)
Comparator: Healthy controls
Design: case-control study
Sample size: 144
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

## Study B
Found: benefit
Claim: Patients with depressive disorder had decreased vitamin D levels compared with healthy controls.
Sentence: "The patients with DD had elevated TXB levels and decreased vitamin D levels, as compared to healthy controls."
Measured as: depressive disorder (vs healthy controls)
Population: Children and adolescents with depressive disorder and healthy controls
Intervention: Baseline vitamin D level (observational comparison)
Comparator: Healthy controls
Design: randomized controlled trial
Sample size: 58
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

## Responses

### Response A
```json
{
 "rationale": "Both compare serum vitamin D between depressed patients and healthy controls but reach opposite conclusions, with adults (mean age ~47) in one and children/adolescents in the other.",
 "verdict": "genuine",
 "reason": "population",
 "also_differs": [
  "design_or_bias"
 ],
 "detail": "population: adults aged 46.9 ± 11 years vs children and adolescents; design: case-control vs a study labeled RCT with n = 58"
}
```

### Response B
```json

 "rationale": "Both studies compare baseline vitamin D levels between patients with depression and healthy controls, but Study A enrolled middle-aged adults treated for depression whereas Study B enrolled children and adolescents.",
 "verdict": "genuine",

}
```

### Response C

 "rationale": "The null association in adults and lower vitamin D levels in depressed children and adolescents genuinely differ, with age being the clearest population difference.",
 "verdict": "genuine",

  "design_or_bias"
 ],
 "detail": "Adults aged 46.9 ± 11 years versus children and adolescents; designs labeled case-control versus randomized controlled trial, although both findings concern observational vitamin D comparisons."
}
